grand_strategy.reading: Tajikistan is a small, poor, landlocked state run as a family business and kept alive by the labour of its men in Russia. Its survival rests on three outside pillars: the Russian garrison and the CSTO, a Chinese creditor and security presence in the Pamirs, and the water and power it hopes to sell downstream. The Taliban are its only open enemy in the region, and the threat Dushanbe fears most - ISIS-K and Tajik jihadists - is also the one that Russia's crackdown on migrants made worse.

stances.note: Treaty alignment: the CSTO (dataset floor, replaced here by the reading) and the 201st base, under a lease agreed in October 2012 to at least 2042, with about 7,000 Russian troops. Friction is visible but does not change the structure: Dushanbe protested the treatment of its citizens in Russia after the Crocus attack (March 2024) and advised them in April 2024 to avoid travel unless necessary, while the migrant economy keeps the two tied. Bond - affinity: Soviet legacy and the Russian language, not a kinship claim. Trend stable: no source calls the alliance cooling; the grade is ours on the treaty and base (confidence B).

stances.note: Transactional: China has been the largest creditor since the late 2000s (Export-Import Bank), with over USD 700m outstanding of about USD 3.04bn at 1 Oct 2026 (Times of Central Asia), though its share was about half in 2016-17 and the drop is unexplained. A Chinese security installation at Shaimak (Murghob, Gorno-Badakhshan) is reported by OSW and by officials quoted by the International Crisis Group; both governments deny a base. No alignment treaty; Chinese workers were killed on the Afghan frontier in November 2025. Bond - none: pure interest. The grade follows the debt and security exchange, not any statement of friendship (confidence C: the base is unconfirmed, the debt is the sourced basis).
